races.long_description: Senator Jeff Merkley is running for re-election in a solidly Democratic state. Among his challengers are State Senator David Brock Smith, a Republican, and Gary Lyndon Dye, a Libertarian.

In a rematch of 2022, Democratic incumbent Tina Kotek faces Christine Drazan, a conservative Republican state legislator. Ms. Kotek’s low approval rating and the state’s slow recovery from the pandemic have made this a closer campaign than the state’s demographics would suggest.
Creates a participatory budgeting system in which residents decide how 2 percent of the city’s annual discretionary budget is spent.

text.paragraph: First results from the state usually come in around 10 p.m. Eastern time. Most voters cast ballots by mail, and full, unofficial counting typically takes days.

Most voters tend to vote early in person, and vote reporting is usually relatively fast. But if a race is very close, it can still take awhile to declare a winner. In 2022, it took until Wednesday afternoon for The A.P. to declare that the top Senate candidates had advanced to a runoff, which was held on Dec. 6.
In 2022 and 2024, about half of the state’s votes were reported by midnight Eastern time on election night, and the count reached 95 percent around 6 a.m. on Wednesday.

In 2024, just under half of voters cast ballots by mail, and it took about two days to report 95 percent of votes statewide. Postmarked ballots must arrive by the fourth day after the election, Nov. 7.
In 2024, 95 percent of the state’s votes were reported just after midnight on election night. Procedural changes could make that even faster this year.

In the past two general elections, 97 percent of the state’s votes were counted by noon Eastern time the day after the election. Counting has sped up since 2020, when it took several days to finish counting mail ballots.

In 2024, 95 percent of the state’s votes were reported by 5 a.m. Eastern time the morning after the election. In some places, absentee ballots are counted at a central facility and reported in large batches.
Most results are typically reported by 1 a.m. Eastern time, and congressional races in recent general elections have been called by The Associated Press on election night.

First results are expected around 1 a.m. Eastern time. In 2024, about 75 percent of votes were reported on election night, and the remaining votes were reported between seven and fifteen days later. Ranked-choice voting is used in federal and state races; if no candidate receives more than 50 percent of the vote, the next tabulation will be conducted on Nov. 18.
Most results are typically reported by early Wednesday morning, and recent congressional races have all been called by The A.P. on election night.

Most voters cast votes by mail, and ballots can take days — or even weeks — to count. Counties have until the 13th day after the election to report their votes, with some exceptions. During the state’s June primaries, this slow process fostered suspicion when two candidates flipped positions five days into vote counting — a phenomenon that is common with election results but usually happens quickly on election night.

The state has long conducted its elections by mail. In 2022 and in 2024, it took about four days to report 95 percent of votes in statewide races. If a race is close, it could take awhile for The A.P. to call a winner.

In 2024, it took a day and a half before 95 percent of votes were counted. But because the state’s congressional races were not especially competitive, they were all called by The A.P. on election night or in the early morning after.
Votes are reported fast, with nearly all ballots counted before midnight in recent elections.

In 2024, about 87 percent of votes were reported by noon Wednesday. The district recently implemented ranked-choice voting, so if no candidate wins more than 50 percent of the vote in certain races, it could take days before additional tabulations are released.
Votes are counted very quickly, with 99 percent of votes reported by midnight in recent general elections. First votes are expected after most polls close at 7 p.m. Eastern time.
The state runs a predominantly mail election. In 2024, it took until about 4 p.m. Eastern time on Wednesday to reach 95 percent of votes. In 2022, it took an additional day.
First results from the state are expected after 11 p.m. Eastern time. In 2022 and 2024, most results were reported by Wednesday afternoon.
In 2024, nearly 95 percent of the state’s votes were reported by noon Eastern time on Wednesday. Ballots postmarked by Election Day have two weeks to arrive.
First results from the state are expected after most polls close at 6 p.m. Eastern time. In 2022 and 2024, most ballots were counted by noon Eastern time on Wednesday.
In 2024, 90 percent of the state’s votes were reported by midnight Eastern time, and 99 percent were in by noon Wednesday. One extremely close House race went to a recount and took weeks to decide.
Most votes were reported by noon Eastern time on Wednesday in 2022 and 2024. Mail ballots have three days to arrive if postmarked by Election Day, but only about one in 10 voters cast them.
First results from the state are expected after most polls close at 6 p.m. Eastern time. In 2024, nearly all votes were counted by midnight on election night.

Most votes are typically reported by midnight Eastern time on election night. Elections for the state’s six U.S. House seats will be open primaries; if no candidate receives a majority of the vote, the top two vote-getters will advance to a Dec. 12 election.

In 2024, it took about a day and a half to reach 95 percent of votes. Ranked choice will be used in the Senate and 2nd Congressional District races, and only first rankings will be available; if no candidate receives a majority, a second tabulation will occur in the days after the election. In 2024, the results of a House race that required a second round were released 10 days after the election.
In 2024, 80 percent of the state’s votes were reported by midnight on election night, and it took several days to reach 95 percent of votes. Ballots postmarked by Election Day have 10 days to arrive.

In 2024, about two-thirds of the state’s votes were reported by midnight on election night, but officials said a longer ballot this year could take more time to process. Ballots postmarked by Election Day have three days to arrive.

In 2024, 56 percent of the state’s votes were reported by midnight Eastern time on election night, and complete unofficial results were in by noon the next day. The deadline for hand-returning absentee ballots on Election Day is now 6 p.m. Eastern time instead of when the polls close.

In 2024, 84 percent of votes were reported by midnight Eastern time on election night. But because the state’s congressional races are not typically competitive, The A.P. tends to call them not long after polls close.
Most results are typically reported by early Wednesday morning, and recent congressional races have all been called by The A.P. on election night.
Most voters cast ballots by mail, which must be received by Election Day. In recent elections, it has taken a day or two to count 95 percent of the votes.
In 2024, about 60 percent of the state’s votes were reported by midnight Eastern time on election night, and 95 percent were in by 5 a.m.
Vote counting was faster in 2024 than in 2022, with three-quarters of the state’s votes reported by midnight on election night, and 93 percent reported by noon the next day.
In 2024, 91 percent of the state’s votes were reported by midnight on election night, and 96 percent were in by noon the next day.

By 1 a.m. Eastern time, processing of absentee ballots must either conclude, or pause and resume the next day. In the last two general elections, nearly all unofficial results were reported by noon Eastern time the day after the election.
Most votes are expected by noon on Wednesday. Mail ballots have a week to arrive if postmarked by Election Day, but only about one in 10 voters cast them in 2024.
In recent general elections, nearly all unofficial results were reported by noon Eastern time on Wednesday.

In recent general elections, 95 percent of votes were reported by midnight Eastern time. Officials expect nearly all unofficial votes to be counted before they leave for the night, because absentee ballots are now due on Election Day instead of four days later (if postmarked). In 2024, it took more than two weeks for the A.P. to call a winner in an extremely close race.
In recent general elections, nearly all votes have been reported by midnight Eastern time on election night.
In recent elections, it has taken more than a week to reach 95 percent of votes counted. The state conducts all-mail elections, and ballots postmarked by Election Day have seven days to arrive.
Most votes are typically counted by around midnight Eastern time on election night.

First results are expected after 9 p.m. Eastern time. More than one-third of voters cast ballots by mail in 2024, and 92 percent of votes were reported by noon Eastern time on Wednesday.
Most votes are typically counted by midnight Eastern time on election night.

In recent elections, 80 to 90 percent of the state’s votes were reported by midnight Eastern time, and 99 percent were in before 7 a.m. the day after the election. Voting by mail requires a valid excuse, and only a small share of voters cast ballots this way.

Most voters cast ballots by mail or dropbox, and it has typically taken more than a week to count 95 percent of votes. New rules requiring officials to verify the last four digits of voters' Social Security or driver's license numbers are expected to extend that timeline.
Nearly all votes are typically counted by noon Eastern time the day after the election.
In recent elections, the state reached 95 percent of votes reported on election night or in the early morning hours after.

In recent general elections, it has taken about eight days to report 95 percent of the state’s votes. Nearly all voters cast ballots by mail or drop box, and ballots with a postmark have 20 days to arrive.

content.text: In an interview on CNN on Wednesday, James Talarico, the Texas Senator-elect, said that his opponent, Ken Paxton, has not called him, but that he watched Paxton’s concession speech on Tuesday night. Talarico said he would be willing to work with all lawmakers regardless of their party, and that he would be willing to vote against his own party. When asked if he would be open to voting to impeach President Trump, Talarico did not answer directly. “I think our top priority has to be delivering for people in Texas,” he said. “They didn’t send us to Washington for political retribution.”

In an illustration of the force of the blue wave that hit Iowa, Eric Armstrong, a Democratic nominee who had suspended his campaign in September, comfortably won his race in a red-leaning State House district, according to the Associated Press. Most Iowa Democrats expected to lose the district after Armstrong
said he was “stepping down”
because personal health issues required “my full attention and care.”
“I’m going to do my best to represent” the district, Armstrong said in a phone interview on Wednesday morning. “But I still have health issues, that’s what I’m struggling with.”

Centrist Democrats announced on Wednesday that they will have at least 14 new members of the moderate Blue Dog Caucus next year, more than doubling the size of the caucus from its current 10 members, with more uncalled races still trending in their favor. The increased numbers will give them more force to counter democratic socialists and progressives who want to influence the agenda next year.

Speaker Mike Johnson told Republican staff on a call this morning that he will not run to lead the House G.O.P. conference in the minority, according to a person familiar with the comments, paving the way for new Republican leadership in the chamber after the party’s drubbing.

The S&P 500 surged higher as exchanges opened for trading. The S&P 500 is up 1.7 percent and the Nasdaq Composite has risen over 2 percent. For investors, more important than who won is that the uncertainty created by the election campaign is over. Even many of the big artificial intelligence companies that could now come under greater scrutiny have risen in early trading.

It looks like Elon Musk deleted his X post on Tuesday morning to “Vote red today!” The post is no longer apparent on his profile as of this morning, and Musk has a tendency to quietly delete social-media messages that don’t hold up well. Doing that would be a mild form of acknowledging the reality that many Americans did not, in fact, vote red. Musk spent nearly $500 million to boost Republicans during the midterms cycle.

The nation shifted towards Democrats by around 15 percentage points in this year’s midterm elections, with much larger swings occurring among subgroups where President Trump made substantial gains only two years ago, like Hispanic voters and voters under 30. Democrats won around 70 percent of the vote with both groups, a much larger advantage than they held with those groups in 2020 or 2024, according to
Times Voter Trends

Ty Masterson, the Republican hoping to flip the Kansas governorship, released a statement that stopped short of conceding but acknowledged a difficult night for Republicans. Masterson is trailing State Senator Cindy Holscher, a Democrat, by more than 5,500 votes, according to The A.P., which has not called the race.

“The first count does not seem to be going our way, but the margin is narrow enough that Kansas law calls for another look, and we’ll let that process finish,” said Masterson, the president of the Kansas Senate.
Stocks initially wobbled on Wednesday as the Democrats’ victory became clear but
have since rallied
, with major benchmarks across Europe rising. The S&P 500 is expected to start trading around 1 percent higher when U.S. exchanges open later this morning.
Even the big A.I. companies expected to come under pressure from potential regulation, or restraints to data center building, nudged higher in pre-market trading.
SpaceX, Elon Musk’s A.I. venture, fell
, pointing to the likely attention to come on Musk’s roles in politics, government and as a business leader.

It was a rough night for the Make America Healthy Again movement, as many candidates aligned with it lost. Zach Lahn — who received a $1 million donation from a PAC associated with the movement, and who appeared alongside Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. last week — was defeated in the Iowa governor’s race. Ken Paxton, who also tied himself to the movement, lost in the Texas Senate race.

Some pro-MAHA candidates pulled through, including Julia Letlow in Louisiana, who was elected to the Senate. Still, the mood among MAHA supporters was bleak. “MAHA moms stayed home and it could’ve swayed some of these races that were unbearably close,” Alex Voetberg, a podcast host and leading voice in the movement, posted on social media.

Some races are still too close to call, leaving some questions unanswered, including how big the Democrats’ House majority will be, and whether the party could further widen its new majority in the Senate. In the Senate, we’re still waiting on results from Mississippi and Alaska. So far, Democrats have gained 19 seats in the House, but
several dozen races have not been called
Times Voter Trends

showed voters across the country and in key Senate races almost uniformly shifted to the left. The Democratic Party’s margin in the national House vote is expected to be about 13 percentage points, the largest for either party in a congressional election in at least a half-century, according to Times estimates. Estimates are based off data from the voter file, election-night precinct results and polling.

Voters across every age group shifted to the left, according to Times Voter Trends. Even voters over the age of 65, a reliably Republican group, shifted to the left this year. White voters without a college degree, another Republican stronghold, also shifted towards the Democrats this year.

content.text: With Democrats having taken control of Congress,
countries around the world

are wondering what comes next for their relationships with the United States. Some students in Tokyo and Sydney expressed hope that the results would check President Trump’s power after two years of disruptive tariffs and a war with Iran, both of which have driven up inflation worldwide. Others questioned whether the results would spur Trump toward more aggressive actions abroad.

Nebraska voters rejected two ballot measures that would have legalized online sports betting in the state. Gambling companies supporting the measures, including DraftKings and FanDuel, poured more than $20 million into the campaign, promising new tax revenue for property tax relief. Opponents, who raised just over $1 million, warned that online betting would threaten the integrity of college sports and fuel gambling addiction.
Nebraska Initiative Measure 440 Election Results: Online Sports Wagering ›

Arizona voters have approved a ballot measure barring transgender student athletes from participating on teams that match their gender identity, The Associated Press reported. The measure also requires transgender students to use only those restrooms and locker rooms that match their sex at birth.
Two traditionally stalwart Democratic groups returned to the party fold these midterms after a dalliance with the G.O.P. in 2024.

Counties with a Black majority had drifted a little more than a percentage point toward Trump two years ago. But when the dust settled this election night, those places moved nearly 16 percentage points toward Democratic Senate candidates. The Democrats ended up beating their Republican opponents by more than 50 percentage points in some counties.

Young voters also appear to have come back to the Democratic fold after some signs they were willing to vote Republican. After counties with large numbers of 18- to 34-year-olds swung more than seven percentage points to Trump in 2024, they swerved left by nearly 23 percentage points this year.
An earlier version of the chart accompanying this article transposed the labels on the data sets. The errors have been fixed.

With Democrats performing so well around the country, the party will be looking at Montana as a big potential missed opportunity. For months, supporters of Seth Bodnar, a well-funded left-leaning independent, and Alani Bankhead, the little-known Democratic nominee, feuded with each other and tried to pressure each other to drop out of the race. In the end, neither did and they split Democratic votes, helping Kurt Alme, the Republican, to an easy victory.

Dan S. Sullivan’s lead in Alaska’s Senate race masks the fact that he is underperforming President Trump’s margins in the 2024 race. Much of the reported vote is from ballots cast on Election Day, which are favorable for Republicans. In the 27 districts that have finished tallying such votes, Sullivan is running behind Trump by an average of 12 percentage points.

In District 22, which includes North Muldoon, one of the most diverse areas in the state, Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate, leads by nearly 20 percentage points among Election Day voters. Trump carried the same district’s day-of vote by nearly four points in 2024. The remaining votes here will be from early and mail ballots, which are expected to lean toward Peltola.

Kurt Alme, a former federal prosecutor, won the Senate race in Montana, according to The Associated Press, allowing Republicans to hold on to an open seat in conservative territory. Alme, the former U.S. attorney for Montana, focused his campaign on reducing federal spending and bringing tax relief.

He entered the race in March after Senator Steve Daines withdrew his candidacy just minutes before the filing deadline. Daines and Gov. Greg Gianforte, a Republican, quickly endorsed Alme, as did President Trump. Some Democrats backed the independent bid of Seth Bodnar over their own nominee, Alani Bankhead, believing he was more electable in the heavily Republican state, and Alme was able to capitalize on the rift.

Representative Marcy Kaptur of Ohio, the longest-serving woman in Congress, defeated Derek Merrin, a Republican, according to The Associated Press, to win her 23rd term. Kaptur, 80, was first elected to the House in 1982. She edged out Merrin two years ago in an area that President Trump carried, and the Ninth Congressional District was redrawn to tilt more conservative. Kaptur prepared for the rematch by moderating her stances to defend her seat. She faced local Democratic backlash over an ad in which she said that “boys should not play in girls’ sports.”

Attorney General Keith Ellison of Minnesota, a Democrat, won a third term, The Associated Press reported, fending off a challenge from a trial lawyer who sought to portray him as complicit in the proliferation of fraud in state-run welfare programs.

Ellison touted the lawsuits his office had filed against the Trump administration, including over its immigration enforcement and pursuit of voter data. He warned that his opponent, Ron Schutz, would be a rubber stamp for the White House.
Adam Hamilton’s victory in the Kansas Senate race represents a significant expansion of the Democrats’ footprint in the state. He carried 11 counties, winning back three that voted Democratic in the
2022 governor’s race
but then flipped to Trump
. He also flipped three counties that voted Republican in both 2022 and 2024.

Turnout in Texas will end in the range of 10 million ballots cast, a record showing for a midterm election in the state that approaches turnout typically seen in a presidential race. It was strongest in areas that James Talarico won, particularly in majority-Hispanic counties like Cameron, Caldwell and Webb, which saw modest declines between 6 percent and 12 percent from two years ago. Midterm turnout often decreases much more sharply.

Richard Pan, a former Democratic state senator, defeated Representative Kevin Kiley, a Republican who changed his registration to independent this year, to win the House seat in a redrawn Northern California district, according to The Associated Press. Pan, a pediatrician who as a state lawmaker was known for passing bills to toughen school vaccine requirements, capitalized in a district where Democrats now outnumber Republicans, 3 to 1. Kiley, who has represented a rural stretch of Northern California in the House since 2022, tried to distance himself from President Trump’s policies.

Mayor Karen Bass of Los Angeles and her democratic socialist challenger, Nithya Raman, were locked in a tight battle with about half of the expected vote counted. The mayor has been in the fight of her political career since last year, when she was out of the country when the Los Angeles wildfires erupted, and the closeness of the early returns was not auspicious for her. Last-minute voting in liberal Los Angeles tends to trend leftward and Raman’s base was largely younger Angelenos, who tend to vote as Election Day gets closer.

Bass, 73, was upbeat as she addressed supporters Tuesday night. “Oh, my goodness! You talk about change,” she said of the Democrats’ resounding success nationwide. “The country has spoken. The city is speaking now.”
Los Angeles Mayor Election Results ›

Elon Musk, who spent a staggering $500 million or so on the midterm elections, weighed in with his first comments on his candidates’ dramatic losses. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he wrote on X. “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.”

We may not know how many ballots remain to be counted in the Mississippi Senate race until next week. The state allows provisional ballots to be counted up to five business days after the election. Around 6,000 were counted in the state in 2022, and about 15,000 in 2024 — both much wider margins than the mere 28 votes that currently separate Scott Colom, the Democrat, and Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican.

Hispanic voters swung to President Trump in 2024, becoming a key demographic that helped push him to victory. But two years into a second term that has heavily focused on deportations, Hispanic voters have decisively shifted against him.

Majority-Hispanic counties moved more than 22 percentage points against Republican Senate candidates, compared with the 2024 presidential election. The change is more than any other major demographic group in the country.
In Kansas and Texas, the swings were dramatic. Majority-Hispanic counties in Kansas swerved 45 percentage points to the left, and those counties in Texas swung almost 36 percentage points.
Notably, the turn was even more dramatic than the 17-percentage-point shift Hispanics made toward Trump just two years ago.

Senator Tommy Tuberville, a former Auburn University football coach who campaigned with harsh anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim rhetoric, will be Alabama’s next governor, according to The Associated Press. He defeated Doug Jones, a former Alabama senator, in a rematch of their Senate fight six years ago.

In Adam Hamilton’s Senate win in Kansas, two counties in the western part of the state — Finney and Seward — shifted around 50 percentage points to the left. Both are majority-Hispanic counties and are home to a large number of meat packing plants. The area is known as the Golden Triangle of Meat Packaging.

Speaker Mike Johnson acknowledged in a statement that Republicans had lost the House, saying that “the American people have made the same decision that has been made in all but two midterms in the last century.”

Former New York City Mayor Mike Bloomberg, who donated over $115 million in September and October to boost Democrats this cycle, shared a statement with The New York Times after the chamber was called for the Democrats. Bloomberg particularly trained his giving on helping Democrats take the House. “Congratulations to Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who will make history as the next Speaker of the House — and the first from New York City. I’m especially glad that so many Moms Demand Action volunteers who stepped up to run won,” Bloomberg said, referring to a group of gun-safety activists he has supported. “I was honored to support their campaigns, and they helped prove that voters across the nation are looking for common sense solutions to the challenges facing the nation.”

Democrats have now snapped Republicans’ governing trifecta, winning key leverage in January over federal spending and oversight. Representative Robert Garcia, the California Democrat who is poised to be the chairman of the Oversight Committee, the main investigative panel in the House, issued a warning in a statement on Tuesday night: “Lawyer up.”
It was long expected that Democrats would retake the House majority, but the scale of their victories tonight has exceeded even the rosiest projections from party officials.
Democrats have won control of the House, The New York Times has projected, giving the party a majority for the final two years of President Trump’s term.

Johnny Garcia, a Democratic former deputy sheriff, prevailed over his Republican rival, Carlos De La Cruz, in a redrawn House district centered in San Antonio, according to The Associated Press. Garcia’s victory defied expectations in a district, Texas’ 35th, that was gerrymandered to favor Republicans last year.

He ran as a conservative Democrat, focusing on economic issues over social ones in a successful bid to defeat De La Cruz, the brother of Representative Monica De La Cruz, a Republican from South Texas.

Democratic socialists are set to have a substantial voice in Congress next year: Members of the Democratic Socialists of America won five House seats in deep-blue districts, joining the two — Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib — already in the House. Two others endorsed by the D.S.A., Angela Gonzales-Torres and Mai Vang, have a chance to join them if they can win their contested California House races.
It’s been a night of rare achievements for Democrats being elected to the Senate.
At least six states elected their first Democratic senator in decades. In
Kansas
, Adam Hamilton became the first Democratic senator elected since 1932. In
Texas
and
Maine
, voters hadn’t elected a Democrat since 1988. In
South Carolina
, they hadn’t elected one since 1998. In
Iowa
and
North Carolina
, voters last elected a Democratic senator in 2008.
And there were several firsts.
New Hampshire
handed a win to Chris Pappas, making him the first openly gay man elected to the Senate.
Minnesota
chose Peggy Flanagan, making her the first Native American woman elected to the Senate.

In South Carolina, Annie Andrews became the first female senator elected in that state (Darline Graham was appointed to the Senate), and Iowa elected Josh Turek, who is expected to become the first former Paralympian U.S. senator.

Areas with large numbers of white residents without college degrees have been major sources of support for Republicans in recent years. But those blue-collar areas shifted sharply toward Democrats this election.

In states with a major Democratic Senate candidate, counties where the majority of the population is white and does not have a bachelor’s degree swung more than 15 percentage points to the left compared with the 2024 election. That’s more than four times the swing to the right they experienced between 2020 and 2024.

Underscoring the importance of those swings, some of the biggest shifts happened in states that ended up having the biggest upsets. In South Carolina, those counties swung by nearly 23 percentage points to the left. In Kansas, the swing was nearly 18 percentage points, and in Iowa the difference was more than 17 percentage points.

House Democrats are also celebrating another milestone tonight: They are on track have more than 100 Democratic women elected to the caucus for the first time in history, an increase of more than 60 percent over the past decade. “Women made history because we showed up to vote and then voted in more than 100 Democratic women to serve in the House,” Representative Teresa Leger Fernandez of New Mexico, the chairwoman of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said in a statement celebrating the milestone.

updates.headline: Update from Ruth Igielnik, Malika Khurana and Zach Levitt

bylines.displayName: Ruth Igielnik, Malika Khurana and Zach Levitt

content.text: Large parts of the country have shifted toward Democrats, averaging about 16 percentage points across the counties that have reported the vast majority of their votes. That is far greater than the roughly five-percentage-point shift toward Republicans in most of the same counties in 2024 when Donald Trump won the presidency.
Even in states where Democrats did not win, voters still shifted sharply to the left from 2024. Results in Tennessee and Kentucky each shifted 18 points toward Democrats.
U.S. Senate Election Results ›

Katy Padilla Stout, a Democrat, decided to run in a sprawling Texas border district to stop a Republican firearms influencer, Brandon Herrera, from representing Uvalde, where 19 children and two teachers were killed in a 2022 school shooting.
Highlighting Herrera’s absolutist views on gun regulations, Padilla Stout pulled off a stunning flip of the 23rd Congressional District, according to The Associated Press.

President Trump won the district by 15 percentage points in 2024. Herrera tried to broaden his appeal by hosting town halls on veterans’ benefits and data centers, but Padilla Stout made his archive of inflammatory online content central to the race, highlighting his offensive jokes about the Holocaust and a demeaning insult about a female gun control activist.
The district has lacked representation since Representative Tony Gonzales withdrew in April because of sexual misconduct allegations.

Republican candidates for governor have lost tonight in red states like Iowa and Texas, but there are a couple of bright spots for them in New England. Gov. Kelly Ayotte has won in New Hampshire after working hard to keep President Trump at arm’s length. And in Vermont — yes, Vermont — the moderate Republican Phil Scott has won a record sixth term.

For a sense of how much the political map of the United States has just been redrawn, consider this: It will be possible to cross the country setting foot only in states that have at least one Democratic senator, except for a 47-mile dash through solid-red Nebraska to get from Percival, Iowa, to Sabetha, Kan.

Your cross-country route might go something like this: Maine to New Hampshire to Vermont to New York to Pennsylvania to Ohio to Michigan to Wisconsin to Iowa, then Kansas to Colorado to Arizona to California.
Before Tuesday’s election, you would have had to cross hundreds of miles of solid-Republican territory — Ohio and Iowa and Nebraska, say, or Kentucky and Missouri and Kansas.

Democrat Troy Jackson defeats Republican Susan Collins to win the race for Senate in Maine, The New York Times projects. Collins survived the last time Democrats won the national vote by double digits — back in 2008 — but she couldn’t hold on tonight.

updates.headline: Update from Nate Cohn, Laura Bult, Nour Idriss, June Kim and Edward Vega

bylines.displayName: Nate Cohn, Laura Bult, Nour Idriss, June Kim and Edward Vega

content.text: Mitchell Berman, a Wisconsin Democrat, upset Representative Bryan Steil, a Republican, to win a House seat based in the state’s southeastern corner, according to The Associated Press.

Berman, an emergency room nurse, won a district that has been a Democratic target for years. Paul Ryan held the seat in the First Congressional District before Steil, a strong fund-raiser whom party officials considered a possible candidate to run for the Senate in 2028 should Senator Ron Johnson not seek a fourth term.
Rebecca Cooke, a Wisconsin Democrat making her third run for Congress, defeated Representative Derrick Van Orden, a hard-line Republican, according to The Associated Press.

Cooke lost to Van Orden in 2024 by fewer than three percentage points, an outcome that showed signs of electability in a rural district that includes several college towns and the city of Eau Claire and went for President Trump the last three presidential cycles.

After that defeat, left-leaning lawmakers like Senators Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Mark Kelly of Arizona started to back Cooke as Democrats’ best chance to flip the seat held by Van Orden, who attended the “Stop the Steal” rally on Jan. 6, 2021, in support of President Trump’s false claim that he had won the 2020 election.

James Talarico’s victory speech hit themes he has hammered throughout his campaign, including that “love is not weak” and that the rich and powerful look to divide people “so we don’t notice that they are picking our pockets.”
He said he would serve, rather than shun, Republicans who opposed him. “This win is not about the Democratic Party or the Republican Party,” he said. “It’s much bigger than that.”
He added that America’s economic and political systems were broken. “That’s because the most powerful people in the world want it that way,” he said.
